A data source is a read-only query a provider answers — an AMI ID, the availability zones, the current account. There is one way in: a **`data` block** in the configuration. That makes `data.<type>.<name>.<attr>` resolvable, and every plan reads it. No tool reads a data source on its own, so to *see* a value:

- **Read the plan.** A read made at plan is in the document's `prior_state` (`show`, which reads `plan.uri`). Planning only to look commits nothing: `cancel` the convergence rather than apply it.
- **Expose it as a root `output`.** After an apply, `output` returns it any time.

```hcl
data "aws_ami" "latest" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["amzn2-ami-hvm-*-x86_64-gp2"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.latest.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
}
```

`count`/`for_each` expand it into keyed instances, with `count.index`/`each.key` in scope. Deleting the block un-declares it: its stored value is pruned at the next apply.

## When it is read

The plan is one dependency-ordered pass over the whole module tree: a data source is read after what it depends on and before what depends on it, across module boundaries. The document shows which kind of read it was:

| In the plan | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prior_state` | Read at plan; the value the plan was computed against |
| `resource_changes[]` with `["read"]` | Moved to apply; `action_reason` says why; counted in `plan.read` |
| `deferred_changes[]` | The provider said "not yet"; a later round reads it |

`up`'s `refresh: false` skips refreshing **managed** objects only: data sources are read at every plan regardless. A read the provider rejects fails the plan with the provider's error.

## Deferred reads

A read that cannot happen at plan moves to apply, as in Terraform:

- **`read_because_config_unknown`** — the query holds a value nothing knows yet (`values = [aws_vpc.main.id]` before the VPC exists). It is read during the apply, once the value exists.
- **`read_because_dependency_pending`** — a `depends_on` target still has a change pending. This is the case unknown-ness misses: a query can be entirely known and still name an object that does not exist yet.

```hcl
data "local_file" "rb" {
  filename   = local_file.note.filename   # known at plan: a literal in local_file.note
  depends_on = [local_file.note]          # without this, the read goes out now and fails
}
```

**The ordering must be declared**: Turf does not infer it from the query, any more than Terraform does. A module call's `depends_on` is inherited by the data sources inside it. Either way nothing in the file needs changing to resolve it: approve the round. What needs the value known at plan (a `count`, a provider block) defers to the next round, which `apply` plans by itself.

## What is stored

State's `data.*` entries are a cache of the last read, as in Terraform. A read is committed when its round applies — the value the plan read, so the apply issues no second read — and a round that failed partway commits the reads it made. A plan that is cancelled or never approved commits nothing. A `destroy` with `refresh` re-reads only the data sources the teardown evaluates (with `refresh: false`, it uses the committed reads), and a completed destroy empties the data namespace with everything else.

For a fresh value — the latest AMI — just run `up` again: every plan re-reads.
